lines.text: Social Security's retirement fund is projected to run dry in 2032.
lines.say: Social Security's retirement fund is projected to run dry in twenty thirty-two.

lines.text: But running dry doesn't mean the checks stop. The real number is 78%.
lines.say: But running dry doesn't mean the checks stop. The real number is seventy-eight percent.

lines.text: That's the projection from Social Security's own Trustees, in their report from June 2026.
lines.say: That's the projection from Social Security's own Trustees, in their report from June twenty twenty-six.

scene.headline: Retirement trust fund projected depleted in late 2032

lines.text: About 70 million people got a Social Security check in December 2025, so that number matters to a lot of kitchen tables.
lines.say: About seventy million people got a Social Security check in December twenty twenty-five, so that number matters to a lot of kitchen tables.

lines.text: Today we'll follow the money from your paycheck to a retiree's mailbox, do the benefit math, and see what 'run out' really means.
lines.say: Today we'll follow the money from your paycheck to a retiree's mailbox, do the benefit math, and see what run out really means.

lines.text: No predictions here. Just the rules, the numbers and the official projections.
lines.say: No predictions here. Just the rules, the numbers and the official projections.

lines.text: Chapter one. Where the money comes from.
lines.say: Chapter one. Where the money comes from.

lines.text: Look at a pay stub and you'll see a line for Social Security. It's 6.2% of your pay.
lines.say: Look at a pay stub and you'll see a line for Social Security. It's six point two percent of your pay.

lines.text: Your employer pays another 6.2% on top. Together that's 12.4%, and self-employed people pay the whole 12.4% themselves.
lines.say: Your employer pays another six point two percent on top. Together that's twelve point four percent, and self-employed people pay the whole twelve point four percent themselves.

lines.text: Here's an example. Someone earning $60,000 pays $3,720 a year, and the employer adds another $3,720.
lines.say: Here's an example. Someone earning sixty thousand dollars pays three thousand, seven hundred twenty dollars a year, and the employer adds another three thousand, seven hundred twenty.

lines.text: That's $7,440 a year going in for one $60,000 worker.
lines.say: That's seven thousand, four hundred forty dollars a year going in for one sixty thousand dollar worker.

lines.text: There's a ceiling, though. In 2026 the tax only applies to the first $184,500 of earnings.
lines.say: There's a ceiling, though. In twenty twenty-six the tax only applies to the first one hundred eighty-four thousand, five hundred dollars of earnings.

lines.text: So the most any worker pays in 2026 is $11,439, no matter how big the salary gets.
lines.say: So the most any worker pays in twenty twenty-six is eleven thousand, four hundred thirty-nine dollars, no matter how big the salary gets.

lines.text: Now the twist most people miss. That money doesn't sit in an account with your name on it.
lines.say: Now the twist most people miss. That money doesn't sit in an account with your name on it.

lines.text: Social Security is mostly pay-as-you-go. The taxes workers pay this month largely fund the checks retirees get this month.
lines.say: Social Security is mostly pay as you go. The taxes workers pay this month largely fund the checks retirees get this month.

lines.text: In 2025, about 185 million people paid into the system, and about 70 million collected from it.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, about one hundred eighty-five million people paid into the system, and about seventy million collected from it.

lines.text: And it's not only retirees. 56 million were retired workers and their families, 8 million were disabled workers and families, and 6 million were survivors.
lines.say: And it's not only retirees. Fifty-six million were retired workers and their families, eight million were disabled workers and families, and six million were survivors.

lines.text: When more comes in than goes out, the extra gets saved in trust funds.
lines.say: When more comes in than goes out, the extra gets saved in trust funds.

lines.text: By law those reserves are held in special US Treasury bonds that pay interest. In 2025 that interest came to $69 billion.
lines.say: By law those reserves are held in special US Treasury bonds that pay interest. In twenty twenty-five that interest came to sixty-nine billion dollars.

lines.text: There are two funds. One pays retirees and survivors, and a smaller one pays disability benefits. Remember that split, it matters later.
lines.say: There are two funds. One pays retirees and survivors, and a smaller one pays disability benefits. Remember that split, it matters later.

lines.text: Chapter two. How your benefit is set.
lines.say: Chapter two. How your benefit is set.

lines.text: First, you have to qualify. Retirement benefits generally take 40 work credits, which is about 10 years of work.
lines.say: First, you have to qualify. Retirement benefits generally take forty work credits, which is about ten years of work.

lines.text: Then Social Security takes your 35 highest-earning years, adjusts older years for wage growth, and averages them per month.
lines.say: Then Social Security takes your thirty-five highest earning years, adjusts older years for wage growth, and averages them per month.

lines.text: That average has a name: A I M E, your average indexed monthly earnings.
lines.say: That average has a name: A I M E, your average indexed monthly earnings.

lines.text: Then comes the formula, and it's tilted on purpose. The first dollars count the most.
lines.say: Then comes the formula, and it's tilted on purpose. The first dollars count the most.

lines.text: For people first eligible in 2026, you get 90% of the first $1,286 of that monthly average.
lines.say: For people first eligible in twenty twenty-six, you get ninety percent of the first one thousand, two hundred eighty-six dollars of that monthly average.

lines.text: Then 32% of the part between $1,286 and $7,749.
lines.say: Then thirty-two percent of the part between one thousand, two hundred eighty-six and seven thousand, seven hundred forty-nine dollars.

lines.text: And just 15% of anything above $7,749. Those two dollar amounts are called bend points.
lines.say: And just fifteen percent of anything above seven thousand, seven hundred forty-nine. Those two dollar amounts are called bend points.

lines.text: Let's run it. Take an example worker whose monthly average, their AIME, comes out to $5,000.
lines.say: Let's run it. Take an example worker whose monthly average, their A I M E, comes out to five thousand dollars.
Step one: ninety percent of one thousand, two hundred eighty-six is one thousand, one hundred fifty-seven dollars and forty cents.

lines.text: Step two: $5,000 minus $1,286 is $3,714. 32% of that is $1,188.48.
lines.say: Step two: five thousand minus one thousand, two hundred eighty-six is three thousand, seven hundred fourteen. Thirty-two percent of that is one thousand, one hundred eighty-eight dollars and forty-eight cents.

lines.text: Nothing is above $7,749, so step three adds zero. The total, rounded down to the dime, is $2,345.80 a month.
lines.say: Nothing is above seven thousand, seven hundred forty-nine, so step three adds zero. The total, rounded down to the dime, is two thousand, three hundred forty-five dollars and eighty cents a month.

lines.text: That replaces about 47% of the worker's average monthly earnings. A high earner gets a bigger check but a smaller share.
lines.say: That replaces about forty-seven percent of the worker's average monthly earnings. A high earner gets a bigger check but a smaller share.

lines.text: For scale, the maximum benefit at full retirement age for someone first eligible in 2026 is $4,152 a month.
lines.say: For scale, the maximum benefit at full retirement age for someone first eligible in twenty twenty-six is four thousand, one hundred fifty-two dollars a month.

scene.label: Max benefit at full retirement age, 2026

lines.text: Now, that $2,345.80 is the amount at full retirement age, which is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.
lines.say: Now, that two thousand, three hundred forty-five dollars and eighty cents is the amount at full retirement age, which is sixty-seven for anyone born in nineteen sixty or later.

lines.text: Claiming changes it. At 62, the check is cut to 70%, which is $1,642.06 in our example.
lines.say: Claiming changes it. At sixty-two, the check is cut to seventy percent, which is one thousand, six hundred forty-two dollars and six cents in our example.

lines.text: At 67, it's the full $2,345.80.
lines.say: At sixty-seven, it's the full two thousand, three hundred forty-five dollars and eighty cents.

lines.text: Wait until 70, and delayed credits of 8% a year push it to 124%, or $2,908.79.
lines.say: Wait until seventy, and delayed credits of eight percent a year push it to a hundred twenty-four percent, or two thousand, nine hundred eight dollars and seventy-nine cents.

lines.text: Same worker, same record. Waiting from 62 to 70 raises the monthly check by $1,266.73 in this example, before any cost-of-living raises.
lines.say: Same worker, same record. Waiting from sixty-two to seventy raises the monthly check by one thousand, two hundred sixty-six dollars and seventy-three cents in this example, before any cost of living raises.

lines.text: Earlier means more checks, later means bigger checks. Which one pays more overall depends on how long someone lives.
lines.say: Earlier means more checks, later means bigger checks. Which one pays more overall depends on how long someone lives.

lines.text: After that, checks rise each year with inflation. The raise was 2.8% for 2026, and our October 13 video breaks down that formula.
lines.say: After that, checks rise each year with inflation. The raise was two point eight percent for twenty twenty-six, and our October thirteenth video breaks down that formula.

scene.label: Cost-of-living raise for 2026
scene.sub: SSA; formula in our Oct 13 video

lines.text: With that raise, the average retired worker's check went from $2,015 to $2,071 a month.
lines.say: With that raise, the average retired worker's check went from two thousand, fifteen dollars to two thousand, seventy-one dollars a month.

lines.text: Chapter three. How we got here.
lines.say: Chapter three. How we got here.

lines.text: Social Security became law on August 14, 1935, in the middle of the Great Depression.
lines.say: Social Security became law on August fourteenth, nineteen thirty-five, in the middle of the Great Depression.

lines.text: When he signed it, President Franklin Roosevelt was upfront about its limits.
lines.say: When he signed it, President Franklin Roosevelt was upfront about its limits.

scene.text: We can never insure one hundred percent of the population against one hundred percent of the hazards and vicissitudes of life

lines.text: The first monthly check went out in January 1940, for $22.54.
lines.say: The first monthly check went out in January nineteen forty, for twenty-two dollars and fifty-four cents.

lines.text: It went to Ida May Fuller of Vermont, and her story is the best illustration of pay-as-you-go ever.
lines.say: It went to Ida May Fuller of Vermont, and her story is the best illustration of pay as you go ever.

lines.text: She paid $24.75 in Social Security taxes. She lived to 100 and collected $22,888.92.
lines.say: She paid twenty-four dollars and seventy-five cents in Social Security taxes. She lived to one hundred and collected twenty-two thousand, eight hundred eighty-eight dollars and ninety-two cents.

lines.text: That only works because younger workers were paying in behind her. The system was built on that chain.
lines.say: That only works because younger workers were paying in behind her. The system was built on that chain.

lines.text: From 1975, checks started rising automatically with inflation.
lines.say: From nineteen seventy-five, checks started rising automatically with inflation.

lines.text: Then came 1983. The retirement fund had been projected to run out in late 1982, and loans from the other funds kept checks going.
lines.say: Then came nineteen eighty-three. The retirement fund had been projected to run out in late nineteen eighty-two, and loans from the other funds kept checks going.

lines.text: Congress passed a package based on a bipartisan commission, and it mixed tax increases with benefit changes.
lines.say: Congress passed a package based on a bipartisan commission, and it mixed tax increases with benefit changes.

lines.text: That's why full retirement age is 67 today instead of 65. And it's why some retirees pay income tax on their checks.
lines.say: That's why full retirement age is sixty-seven today instead of sixty-five. And it's why some retirees pay income tax on their checks.

lines.text: The 1983 law also helped the trust funds build a big cushion, because the baby boomers were still working and paying in.
lines.say: The nineteen eighty-three law also helped the trust funds build a big cushion, because the baby boomers were still working and paying in.

lines.text: Chapter four. The trust fund math.
lines.say: Chapter four. The trust fund math.

lines.text: Now the boomers are retiring, and the cushion is being spent. Here's 2025.
lines.say: Now the boomers are retiring, and the cushion is being spent. Here's twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: In 2025 the program took in $1.449 trillion, including interest, and spent $1.609 trillion.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five the program took in one point four four nine trillion dollars, including interest, and spent one point six oh nine trillion.

lines.text: Most of that income was payroll tax, $1.323 trillion. Income tax on benefits added $58 billion, and interest $69 billion.
lines.say: Most of that income was payroll tax, one point three two three trillion dollars. Income tax on benefits added fifty-eight billion, and interest sixty-nine billion.

lines.text: The gap was covered from savings. The trust funds shrank by $160 billion in one year.
lines.say: The gap was covered from savings. The trust funds shrank by a hundred sixty billion dollars in one year.

lines.text: Zoom out, and here are the combined reserves at the end of each year since 2015, in billions of dollars.
lines.say: Zoom out, and here are the combined reserves at the end of each year since twenty fifteen, in billions of dollars.

scene.title: Social Security trust fund reserves ($B, year-end)

lines.text: They peaked at $2,908 billion at the end of 2020. Every year since, they've gotten smaller.
lines.say: They peaked at two thousand, nine hundred eight billion dollars at the end of twenty twenty. Every year since, they've gotten smaller.

lines.text: From that peak to the end of 2025, that's $347 billion drawn down.
lines.say: From that peak to the end of twenty twenty-five, that's three hundred forty-seven billion dollars drawn down.

lines.text: Why? The simplest picture is the number of workers paying in for each person collecting.
lines.say: Why? The simplest picture is the number of workers paying in for each person collecting.

lines.text: In 1960, there were about 5.1 workers for every beneficiary. In 2025, about 2.6.
lines.say: In nineteen sixty, there were about five point one workers for every beneficiary. In twenty twenty-five, about two point six.

lines.text: And the Trustees project it falls to about 1.9 by 2075, as people live longer and families have fewer kids.
lines.say: And the Trustees project it falls to about one point nine by twenty seventy-five, as people live longer and families have fewer kids.

lines.text: In fact, the 2026 report lowered its long-run fertility assumption from 1.90 to 1.75 children per woman.
lines.say: In fact, the twenty twenty-six report lowered its long-run fertility assumption from one point nine oh to one point seven five children per woman.

lines.text: Another change came from the 2025 tax law. It added a temporary extra deduction for people 65 and older.
lines.say: Another change came from the twenty twenty-five tax law. It added a temporary extra deduction for people sixty-five and older.

lines.text: Less income tax on benefits means less money flowing back into the trust funds, and the Trustees counted that too.
lines.say: Less income tax on benefits means less money flowing back into the trust funds, and the Trustees counted that too.

lines.text: Chapter five. What run out really means.
lines.say: Chapter five. What run out really means.

lines.text: Here's the headline from the June 2026 report. The retirement fund is projected to be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032.
lines.say: Here's the headline from the June twenty twenty-six report. The retirement fund is projected to be depleted in the fourth quarter of twenty thirty-two.

lines.text: Last year's report said 2033, so the date moved up by about one quarter.
lines.say: Last year's report said twenty thirty-three, so the date moved up by about one quarter.

lines.text: But depleted means the savings are gone, not the taxes. Workers keep paying in every payday.
lines.say: But depleted means the savings are gone, not the taxes. Workers keep paying in every payday.

lines.text: So after 2032, incoming money is projected to cover 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits.
lines.say: So after twenty thirty-two, incoming money is projected to cover seventy-eight percent of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits.

lines.text: Remember the disability fund? It's projected to pay full benefits through at least 2100.
lines.say: Remember the disability fund? It's projected to pay full benefits through at least twenty one hundred.

lines.text: If lawmakers combined the two funds, the Trustees project they'd last until the third quarter of 2034, then pay 83%.
lines.say: If lawmakers combined the two funds, the Trustees project they'd last until the third quarter of twenty thirty-four, then pay eighty-three percent.

lines.text: Why a cut and not a loan? Under current law, the trust funds have no authority to borrow.
lines.say: Why a cut and not a loan? Under current law, the trust funds have no authority to borrow.

lines.text: So unless Congress changes the law first, benefits would be limited to what's coming in.
lines.say: So unless Congress changes the law first, benefits would be limited to what's coming in.

lines.text: Let's put that on our example worker. 78% of $2,345.80 is $1,829.72 a month.
lines.say: Let's put that on our example worker. Seventy-eight percent of two thousand, three hundred forty-five dollars and eighty cents is one thousand, eight hundred twenty-nine dollars and seventy-two cents a month.

lines.text: That's $516.08 less every month, or about 22%. That's the gap behind the scary headlines.
lines.say: That's five hundred sixteen dollars and eight cents less every month, or about twenty-two percent. That's the gap behind the scary headlines.

lines.text: So 'Social Security will disappear' isn't what the projection says. A cut in the low 20s, if nothing changes, is what it says.
lines.say: So Social Security will disappear isn't what the projection says. A cut in the low twenties, if nothing changes, is what it says.

lines.text: Chapter six. The ways to close the gap.
lines.say: Chapter six. The ways to close the gap.

scene.title: The ways to close the gap

lines.text: The Trustees measure the long-run hole over 75 years. In the 2026 report it's 4.42% of taxable payroll.
lines.say: The Trustees measure the long-run hole over seventy-five years. In the twenty twenty-six report it's four point four two percent of taxable payroll.

lines.text: To close it with taxes alone, starting in 2026, the payroll tax would go from 12.4% to 16.65%.
lines.say: To close it with taxes alone, starting in twenty twenty-six, the payroll tax would go from twelve point four percent to sixteen point six five percent.

lines.text: To close it with benefit cuts alone, every current and future beneficiary would get 25.2% less.
lines.say: To close it with benefit cuts alone, every current and future beneficiary would get twenty-five point two percent less.

lines.text: Or, if current retirees were protected, cuts for people newly eligible in 2026 and later would be 30.3%.
lines.say: Or, if current retirees were protected, cuts for people newly eligible in twenty twenty-six and later would be thirty point three percent.

lines.text: For our $60,000 example worker, 16.65% would mean $9,990 a year in total payroll tax, instead of $7,440.
lines.say: For our sixty thousand dollar example worker, sixteen point six five percent would mean nine thousand, nine hundred ninety dollars a year in total payroll tax, instead of seven thousand, four hundred forty.

lines.text: Real proposals usually mix things: raising the $184,500 cap, changing the retirement age, adjusting the formula, or new revenue.
lines.say: Real proposals usually mix things: raising the one hundred eighty-four thousand, five hundred dollar cap, changing the retirement age, adjusting the formula, or new revenue.

lines.text: Each one moves the cost onto someone: workers, employers, higher earners, future retirees or taxpayers in general.
lines.say: Each one moves the cost onto someone: workers, employers, higher earners, future retirees or taxpayers in general.

lines.text: Which mix is fair is a political choice, and we're not picking sides. The math just says the sooner a fix starts, the smaller each piece can be.
lines.say: Which mix is fair is a political choice, and we're not picking sides. The math just says the sooner a fix starts, the smaller each piece can be.

lines.text: And 1983 shows Congress has acted right up against a deadline before.
lines.say: And nineteen eighty-three shows Congress has acted right up against a deadline before.

lines.text: Chapter seven. The recap.
lines.say: Chapter seven. The recap.

lines.text: Workers and employers each pay 6.2%, up to $184,500 in 2026, and most of it goes straight out as today's checks.
lines.say: Workers and employers each pay six point two percent, up to one hundred eighty-four thousand, five hundred dollars in twenty twenty-six, and most of it goes straight out as today's checks.

lines.text: Your check comes from your top 35 years, a tilted formula, and the age you claim.
lines.say: Your check comes from your top thirty-five years, a tilted formula, and the age you claim.

lines.text: The trust funds peaked in 2020 and fell $160 billion in 2025 alone, as fewer workers support each beneficiary.
lines.say: The trust funds peaked in twenty twenty and fell a hundred sixty billion dollars in twenty twenty-five alone, as fewer workers support each beneficiary.

lines.text: And if Congress doesn't act, the Trustees project 78% of retirement benefits payable after late 2032, not zero.
lines.say: And if Congress doesn't act, the Trustees project seventy-eight percent of retirement benefits payable after late twenty thirty-two, not zero.

lines.text: So will Social Security run out? The savings are projected to. The program itself, funded by every paycheck, keeps going.
lines.say: So will Social Security run out? The savings are projected to. The program itself, funded by every paycheck, keeps going.

lines.text: Your own estimate, based on your real earnings record, is on your my Social Security account at ssa.gov.
lines.say: Your own estimate, based on your real earnings record, is on your my Social Security account at S S A dot gov.

post.title: Social Security's fund is projected to run dry in 2032. Here's what that really means.
post.ig: Social Security's retirement fund is projected to run dry in 2032. But the checks don't go to zero.
post.tiktok: Social Security 'running out' in 2032 doesn't mean what you think. The real number is 78%.
post.yt_desc:
Social Security's retirement trust fund is projected to be depleted in late 2032, according to the Trustees Report released June 9, 2026. But depleted doesn't mean zero: incoming payroll taxes are projected to cover about 78% of scheduled benefits after that. We follow the money from the 6.2% payroll tax to the monthly check, work through the 2026 benefit formula step by step, and look at 90 years of history and the trade-offs in the options to close the gap. No predictions, just the rules, the numbers and the official projections.
